This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples

question: Why would large dot products push the softmax into regions with tiny gradients?
text:
Ask
¶21

Why would large dot products push the softmax into regions with tiny gradients?

Because softmax saturates when one logit dwarfs the rest. With large d_k, dot products grow in magnitude (variance d_k, per footnote 4 in ¶23), so one score dominates. Softmax then outputs nearly 1 for that entry and nearly 0 for others, and its gradient with respect to the logits goes to zero there, so learning stalls. Dividing by √d_k rescales the scores back to a sane range ¶21.

text:
Ask
¶61

What is label smoothing, and why would it help BLEU while hurting perplexity?

Label smoothing replaces the hard one-hot target with a soft distribution, so the model is trained to assign a little probability mass to wrong tokens instead of chasing 1.0 on the right one. That makes it less confident, which is exactly why perplexity (a measure of how sharply it predicts the true token) gets worse ¶61.

BLEU rewards the actual decoded sentence, and a less overconfident model generalizes better and picks better sequences. The text states the trade-off without explaining the mechanism; the calibration argument is outside it.

What does a beam size of 4 mean in practice?

It means the decoder keeps the 4 most promising partial translations alive at each step, not just the single best one. question: What limitations of the Transformer do the authors themselves acknowledge?
text:
Whole text
¶63

What limitations of the Transformer do the authors themselves acknowledge?

The authors acknowledge few limitations, and mostly as trade-offs rather than flaws.

Reduced effective resolution: constant-path attention averages attention-weighted positions, which they counteract with Multi-Head Attention ¶7.
Cost grows with sequence length: self-attention is O(n²·d), so it only beats recurrent layers when n < d; for very long sequences they propose restricting attention to a neighborhood of size r ¶49¶50.
Positional encoding is a patch: since there is no recurrence or convolution, order must be injected artificially ¶40.
They note a more sophisticated compatibility function than dot product may help ¶75.

Outside the text: later work (Longformer, Performer, and similar) targets exactly the quadratic-length limit.

text:

¶63

Which ablation results in Table 3 matter most, and why?

Rows (A) and (D) matter most. Row (A) is the one ablation that justifies the paper's central claim: multi-head attention beats single-head by 0.9 BLEU, and quality falls off again at 32 heads ¶75. That is the empirical case for the architecture, not just for attention. Row (D) shows dropout is essential (24.6 without it versus 25.5 with), which is why the base model's numbers are credible rather than overfit ¶75.

Row (E) is the quiet one: learned positional embeddings tie the sinusoids, so the sinusoidal choice rests on an extrapolation hypothesis, not a measured gain ¶75.

Gloss
8 parts · 5 claims · 3 caveats

The paper argues that sequence transduction can be done with an encoder-decoder architecture built entirely from attention, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions, and that this Transformer trains faster and translates better. It matters because it sets new WMT 2014 translation results and shows attention-only models can generalize to constituency parsing.

Key claims
1

The paper proposes the Transformer, an encoder-decoder architecture based solely on attention mechanisms and dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. ¶2

2

Self-attention layers connect all positions with O(1) sequential operations and O(1) maximum path length, while recurrent layers require O(n) sequential operations and O(n) path length. ¶39

3

Multi-head attention uses h=8 parallel attention layers with d_k=d_v=64, concatenating their outputs and projecting them to let the model attend to different representation subspaces. ¶29

4

On WMT 2014 English-to-German newstest2014, Transformer (big) scores 28.4 BLEU, above ConvS2S Ensemble's 26.36 and GNMT + RL Ensemble's 26.30. ¶60

5

On WMT 2014 English-to-French newstest2014, Transformer (big) scores 41.8 BLEU, above ConvS2S Ensemble's 41.29 and GNMT + RL Ensemble's 41.16. ¶60

Keep in mind

The prose says the big English-to-French model achieves 41.0 BLEU ¶65, which disagrees with Table 2's 41.8 ¶60. ¶65

The prose claims the base model surpasses all previously published models and ensembles ¶65, but Table 2 shows its English-to-French 38.1 BLEU is below GNMT + RL 39.92, ConvS2S 40.46 and MoE 40.56 ¶60. ¶65

The parsing results are not uniformly state of the art: Transformer scores 91.3 F1 on WSJ only versus Dyer et al.'s 91.7, and 92.7 semi-supervised versus Dyer et al.'s 93.3 ¶78. ¶78

Fact-check
¶50

self-attention could yield more interpretable models

Partly. The claim survives as a research program, not as a settled fact. The paper's own evidence is anecdotal: attention heads in layer 5 seem to track long-distance dependencies and anaphora ¶133¶134¶136, which is suggestive, not proof.

Outside the text, later work complicated the picture. Attention weights can be unstable explanations, and methods like effective attention, which strips out the value matrix, give different and arguably more faithful readings 5; attribution methods such as AttAttr were proposed precisely because raw attention is an incomplete account of information flow 2. Human-grounded evaluations find attention-based explanations roughly on par with SHAP and LIME on some tasks, not clearly better 4.

Confidence: moderate. The interpretability claim is contested, and the field has not converged.
